definition: Truculent means aggressively defiant; eager to fight.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word truculent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know truculent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The film's mechanic is truculent from her first line, answering a customer's 'good morning' with 'want to make something of it?'
Prickly people bristle when handled wrong, but that is far from truculent's open hunt for a fight.
Quarrelsome picks verbal fights over anything; it stops short of truculent, which is ready to make the fight physical.

Belligerent means ready for battle — hostility already on a war footing, whether between nations or in a bar. Truculent adds eagerness and display: the truculent person is not merely prepared for a fight but visibly hoping for one, disappointed when peace breaks out.

Feisty means scrappy and spirited, and it is usually said with admiration — the small dog, the underdog, the grandmother who will not be talked over. Truculent has lost the charm: its defiance is aggressive, spoiling for a real fight rather than showing likable spunk.
quietly submissive; slow to defend even oneself
disposed to avoid quarrels altogether

Latin trux, 'savage,' entered English exactly once, inside truculent. Despite the sound, it is no relation to truce — an Old English word for a pledge of peace, nearly its opposite — or to truck. The -ulent ending, though, is the same 'full of' you see in turbulent and fraudulent.
Truculent means aggressively defiant; eager to fight.
Even in the retirement home's chess club, Mr.
Baxter stays truculent, offering to settle stalemates 'the old way' until the nurses wheel him in to lunch.
Truculent is more than grouchy: it is aggression looking for an outlet, defiance that hopes you will push back.
A surly person wants to be left alone; a truculent one is disappointed when the argument ends peacefully.
Truculent is for open, eager-to-fight defiance — a posture you can see across a room.
Surly is unfriendly but passive; quarrelsome argues; truculent squares up.
Malevolent (this unit) is darker: it wishes harm quietly, while truculent announces itself.

Everyone at the Elm Street garden knew within a week that the new plot-holder, Mr.
Vance, was truculent by temperament rather than by grievance.
He did not wait to be wronged.

He measured his neighbors' fences with a tape and dared anyone to object, and posted a sign inviting complaints to be made 'in person, anytime.' When the water schedule came out fair, he seemed almost let down; he read it twice, looking for the insult that wasn't there.
The garden president tried a peace offering — a flat of tomato starts left at his gate.
Vance returned it with a note: 'I know what you're doing.' By August the committee understood that he wasn't defending anything.
He simply liked the wind-up before a fight, and was gloomy in every season of calm.
